raw_case_text:
Patient 2 was a 15-year-old Peruvian boy seen in September 2001 with a 1-year history of headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive deterioration in visual function. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan performed in April 2001 showed several large, irregular enhancing mass lesions involving the left occipital and parietal lobes (Figure 2). He had come to the United States in September for further evaluation. On neurologic examination, the patient had a right homonymous hemianopsia, optic nerve atrophy, and major visual impairment (left eye:20/100; right eye:20/200). Repeat MRI showed several irregular areas of enhancement in the left parietooccipital area associated with marked brain edema, left-to-right shift, and mass effect (Figure 2).
The patient was taken to surgery, where a firm avascular mass was found beneath a 0.5-cm layer of softer gliotic cortical tissue. Frozen sections showed lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with granuloma formation. Specimens for cultures and histopathologic examination were obtained. Bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Final histopathologic examination showed numerous granulomas with multinucleated giant cells but no organisms (Figure 1).
Serologic test results for Brucella, T. gondii, and Taenia soleum were negative. On postoperative day 8, mycobacteria cultures (BacT/ALERT MP; Organon Teknika Corp., Durham, NC) showed growth of a gram-negative coccobaccillus, later confirmed as Brucella spp. Treatment with rifampin, doxycycline, and intravenous gentamicin was begun. After 1 week, the gentamicin was discontinued per current recommendations, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was started. Follow-up imaging 7 months later demonstrated resolution of the enhancing areas and edema, with residual areas of brain atrophy (Figure 2). The patient's vision improved, but some visual acuity deficits persisted. Anti-brucella therapy continued for 1 year.
The patient lived in a small town 7 hours from Lima and had not traveled outside of the country before coming to the United States. His diet included regular consumption of queso fresco and occasional ceviche but no other raw meats. He reported no direct contact with marine mammals and seldom visited the Peruvian coast.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old Peruvian male presented with a 1-year history of headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive visual deterioration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive headaches, nausea, vomiting, and worsening visual function over a 1-year period. Brain MRI in April 2001 revealed enhancing intracranial masses. He traveled to the United States in September 2001 for further evaluation and neurosurgical intervention.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of a small Peruvian town 7 hours from Lima; had not traveled outside Peru prior to entering the United States. Dietary/epidemiological history: regular consumption of queso fresco (unpasteurized cheese) and occasional ceviche; denied consuming other raw meats; no direct contact with marine mammals and seldom visited the Peruvian coast.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports headaches, nausea, vomiting, and progressive decline in vision. Denies other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Neurologic examination revealed right homonymous hemianopsia, optic nerve atrophy, and severe visual impairment (visual acuity: left eye 20/100; right eye 20/200).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (April 2001) showed several large, irregular enhancing mass lesions in the left occipital and parietal lobes. Repeat brain MRI (September 2001) showed multiple irregular areas of enhancement in the left parietooccipital area with marked brain edema, left-to-right shift, and mass effect. Craniotomy revealed a firm avascular mass beneath a 0.5-cm layer of gliotic cortex; frozen section showed lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with granuloma formation; final histopathology demonstrated numerous granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and no visible organisms; bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Follow-up brain MRI at 7 months demonstrated resolution of enhancing areas and edema with residual localized brain atrophy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: On postoperative day 8, tissue mycobacterial culture bottles (BacT/ALERT MP) yielded a gram-negative coccobacillus, confirmed as Brucella spp., establishing the diagnosis of neurobrucellosis presenting as multifocal intracranial brucellomas. Initial serologic tests for Brucella, Toxoplasma gondii, and Taenia solium were negative. Differential diagnoses ruled out: Toxoplasmosis, neurocysticercosis, and tuberculosis excluded by negative serologies and stains. Management and Outcome: Treated with surgical debulking and medical therapy initiating oral rifampin, oral doxycycline, and IV gentamicin for 1 week; gentamicin was then replaced with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), and antimicrobial therapy was continued for a total duration of 1 year. The patient experienced partial recovery of visual function (with some persistent visual acuity deficits), and 7-month follow-up imaging confirmed complete resolution of cerebral lesions and edema.
